claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially homogeneous and single-phase BCC at high temperature.
Phase instability in this alloy arises from competition between thermodynamic ordering tendencies and kinetic limitations caused by differential atomic diffusivities.
Cr and Al diffuse more slowly than Co, Fe, and Ni in this alloy.
During cooling, differential diffusion produces local chemical inhomogeneities.
Local chemical inhomogeneities trigger ordering or secondary-phase precipitation from the high-temperature BCC structure.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature exposure permits fast-diffusing elements to redistribute ahead of slow-diffusing elements.
The resulting elemental segregation lowers the free energy for nucleation of new phases.
Rapid quenching suppresses elemental redistribution and preserves the metastable high-temperature BCC phase.
A rapidly quenched reference sample will remain predominantly single-phase BCC.
Relative to the quenched baseline, slowly cooled or thermally exposed samples will develop secondary ordered or precipitated phases.
The amount and nature of secondary phases will correlate with cooling rate and thermal-exposure duration.
The proposed behavior applies when cooling or annealing provides sufficient atomic mobility for differential diffusion.
The proposed behavior should not apply during sufficiently rapid quenching or at temperatures where diffusion is effectively frozen.
The identity of the secondary phases depends on thermodynamic factors not specified by composition alone.
Absence of measurable secondary phases or local chemical ordering after slow cooling or thermal exposure, relative to the quenched control, would falsify the hypothesis.
